Settlement.name: {=Settlements.Settlement.name.castle_LT12}Upite
Settlement.text: {=Settlements.Settlement.text.castle_LT12}The name Upytė was first mentioned in 1254 in a Livonian chronicle dealing with the divisions of the Upmala region. Upytė had a wooden castle built on an island which later became a hillfort when Lake Vešeta was drained. The castle was an important northern defence post against numerous incursions of the Livonian Order.

Settlement.name: {=town_POL1}Gdansk
Settlement.text: {=town_POL1.text}In the 13th century, Gdańsk stood as a prosperous Baltic port city and trading center under the rule of Pomeranian dukes, with its wooden and earthen fortifications protecting the bustling settlement. The city's strategic location at the mouth of the Vistula River made it a crucial meeting point for merchants from across the Baltic and Central Europe, where Slavic traders mingled with German merchants and other seafarers in its growing harbor district.

Settlement.name: {=town_POL2}Plotsk
Settlement.text: {=town_POL2_text}In the 13th century, Plock served as one of the most significant centers of Masovia, functioning both as a major ecclesiastical seat with its impressive cathedral and as a crucial political center for the Masovian dukes. The city's strategic location on the high bank of the Vistula River enhanced its importance as a trade hub, while its strong fortifications, including a castle on the hill, helped protect it during the tumultuous period of feudal divisions in medieval Poland.

Settlement.name: {=town_SW1}Visby
Settlement.text: {=town_SW1_desc}The wealthy merchant city of Visby dominates the Baltic trade, its German and Gutnish merchants controlling the flow of furs, amber, and silver between Scandinavia, the Hanseatic cities, and Novgorod. Though nominally independent, tensions simmer between the cosmopolitan urban elite and the traditional Gutnish farmers who see their ancient freedoms threatened by foreign wealth and influence.
